newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea puts exit ban on bankers, raid Hanbo Steel.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea puts exit ban on bankers, raid Hanbo Steel.

text.p: South Korean police raided the home and offices of the founder of the Hanbo Group on Tuesday, and a travel ban was slapped on four top bankers who extended huge loans to the company's failed steel unit.
Police seized documents belonging to Chung Tae-soo, who built South Korea's 14th largest industrial conglomerate now wallowing in a sea of debt.
President Kim Young-sam on Monday ordered a thorough investigation into $5.8 billion of loans funnelled to Hanbo Steel Co despite its shaky condition.
A prosecution official said police stormed into the personal office and home of Chung and offices of Hanbo Steel and 15 other affiliates to hunt for loan-related documents.
"Search warrants were issued to seize evidence for any financial irregularities," prosecutor Lee Chung-soo said.
Hanbo Steel filed for court receivership to protect it from creditors. The country's second largest steelmaker defaulted on its debt repayments last week.
The group's trading arm, Hanbo Corp, also sought court protection and two other units are scheduled to follow.
The steelmaker, now building a huge new facility in the southern town of Tangjin, borrowed five trillion won ($5.8 billion) from 61 banks and financial institutions, about 20 times its net worth.
"The government today imposed an overseas travel ban on a further 17 people, including the heads of the four banks, over the Hanbo investigation," a Justice Ministry official said.
The banks are Korea First Bank, Cho Hung Bank, Korea Exchange Bank and unlisted Korea Development Bank, which have the biggest exposure to Hanbo Steel.
This brings to 29 the total number of people banned from leaving the country over Hanbo's loan scandal, he added. Others include Chung himself and other Hanbo executives.
It is not the first time Chung has been investigated.
He paid 15 billion won into a slush fund raised by former president Roh Tae-woo, now serving a 17-year jail term for corruption and human rights abuses.
But a Seoul court trying Chung and Roh, along with other tycoons, acquitted Chung on the grounds the money was forcibly extracted.
Opposition parties say the Hanbo loans are the biggest financial scandal in the country's history and must have involved government favours.
The ruling New Korea Party said its parliamentary leader met his opposition counterparts to discuss reopening the National Assembly for talks on Hanbo.

The scandal again hammered the stock market on Tuesday, with banking and securities shares losing heavily. The main index lost 1.85 points to end at 662.85, despite measures by the government to boost sentiment.
The central bank said it would inject another 600 billion won into the banking system on Tuesday to prevent a credit crunch.
This followed injections of a total of three trillion won on Monday and last Friday.
An outlawed union organisation said it was abandoning once-a-week strikes on Wednesdays, partly due to economic turmoil caused by the Hanbo collapse.

But the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions still planned to go ahead with full stoppages starting on February 18 unless the government scrapped a controversial new labour law, a union official said.
"Korea is in turmoil due to the Hanbo incident and we have taken that into consideration," said the official.
The confederation led almost four weeks of industrial stoppages against new legislation after it was rammed through parliament on December 26.
President Kim was forced into a humiliating retreat and sent the bill back to parliament for revision. But Kim has ruled out voiding the bill.
